body.heading: Thanks with dirt on it
paragraphs: Harvest festivals are among humanity’s oldest celebrations. Thanksgiving in North America centres on a shared feast of gratitude; Germany’s Erntedankfest thanks God and community for the gathered crops, often with processions and decorated churches; in China and Vietnam, the Mid-Autumn Festival pairs the harvest moon with family reunion and mooncakes. Different tables, same astonishment: the earth provided, again.
Original gratitude was not a mood. It was a response to survival, said out loud, together, over food.

body.heading: Gratitude that names its sources
paragraphs: Harvest thanks is specific by nature: this field, this rain, these hands. That specificity is what modern gratitude practice keeps rediscovering — thanks that names its object lands differently from a general glow of appreciation.
It also remembers the labour. Behind every harvest table stand planters, pickers, drivers, and cooks, most of them unnamed. Naming the chain, even briefly, is part of the thanks.

body.heading: A harvest of your own
paragraphs: Your household has harvests too: the project finished, the exam survived, the garden’s three heroic tomatoes. Mark one each year with a deliberate meal and one spoken sentence of thanks that names what actually made it possible.
Gratitude kept seasonal and spoken has a way of surviving the winter.

takeaway: Make gratitude seasonal, spoken, and specific — naming the field, the rain, and the hands.
